prospect.name: Jeffrey Silver
prospect.occupation: Works full-time in a hospital; the specific role is never asked and never stated. Sedentary desk work with stair-climbing between floors. One-hour commute each way, in the office 09:00-17:00.
prospect.family_status: Married; eats out or orders in with his wife three to four nights a week. Has an adult daughter who is a physical therapist and who has already assessed his movement. Owns a dog.
prospect.training_background: Extensive but lapsed. Has run half marathons, played sports, worked with personal trainers, and trained martial arts for five to six years. For the past two to three years only home yoga, calisthenics, push-ups, sit-ups, dips, squats and side lunges from Instagram and Facebook programmes, plus a daily two-mile dog walk. Describes the real decline as roughly five years: 'I really have not been, I haven't trained or anything in about five years now.' Currently 8,500-11,000 steps a day and 15-30 minutes of home work most mornings.
prospect.medical: SUBSTANTIAL SURGICAL HISTORY, ALL DISCLOSED IN RESPONSE TO A DIRECT QUESTION. (1) Right ankle reconstruction, which limits dorsiflexion at that joint. (2) Bilateral knee problems — 'squatting, I can't squat all that much', and the knees 'ache and they pop'. (3) Cervical fusion of the neck, which he says causes him no current issues. (4) Progressive loss of muscle mass over two to five years, concentrated in the glutes and legs, with associated belly fat — presenting as sarcopenia at 68. (5) Mild lower-back stiffness, no pain. (6) Sleeps around seven hours, 22:00 to 05:00, waking once a night to urinate and sometimes then sleeping fitfully; variable sleep score. (7) Increased fatigue over the past year. His daughter, a physical therapist, has already identified a movement pattern issue: 'my mobility, my lack of mobility, I don't trigger my glutes. I trigger my quads when I do stuff more than my glutes.' Nutrition is Herbalife-based: two meal-replacement shakes daily, two protein snacks, one dinner, no alcohol, no sweetened drinks. NOTE: no health-condition, medication, blood-pressure or cardiac question was asked, and no clinician clearance was sought or suggested at any point.

notable.note: The most serious clinical omission in the batch, and it is not a screening failure — it is a follow-through failure. The rep asked the injury question properly and thoroughly, and a 68-year-old told him he has had an ankle reconstruction limiting dorsiflexion, bilateral knee problems that prevent squatting, and a cervical fusion of the neck. The rep's response to the summary of that picture was 'That's great. That's great.' He then sold six months of loaded ballistic kettlebell training without asking whether a clinician would clear it, without asking what the restrictions mean in practice, and without suggesting the prospect's own daughter — a physical therapist who has already assessed his movement — be consulted. Cervical fusion and overhead kettlebell work is the specific combination that should have stopped this call. Two other things: the rep heard 'I do not have that right now, so I can't retire' and never connected it to the $6,000 ask fourteen minutes later; and he declined to send a payment link to a prospect who had verbally agreed and asked for one, which cost him the momentum and produced a postponement request within thirty minutes.
